accumulator-loop.caption: Start the running total at zero.
The first value supplied by range(3) is 0.
Store the result back in total. Its value is still 0.
The next iteration sets n to 1. The total is retained.
The third iteration sets n to 2. The total is still 1.
range(3) has no more values. Execution leaves the loop.
Look up the final total to print it.
The console shows 3, the sum of 0, 1, and 2.

boolean-comparisons.caption: A comparison asks a question about values. Is 2 less than 3?
Yes. The comparison produces True, a Boolean value, rather than another number.
The console shows True, the result of the first comparison.
Now ask whether 2 equals 3. The == operator compares values; it does not assign a value to a name.
The values are not equal, so this comparison produces False. Both results have the bool type.
The second console line shows False. Conditions can use these Boolean results to decide what runs next.

changing-value.caption: Read the old value of score on the right-hand side first. It is still 5.
Adding 2 gives 7. This is the new result, but score still holds 5 until assignment happens.
Now bind score to the result 7, replacing its previous value. This is an assignment, not an algebraic equality.
The console shows the updated value 7.

class-instance.caption: Student has an initializer named __init__. No Student instance exists yet; the initializer runs when we create one.
Evaluate the argument "Ada" before constructing a Student.
Allocate a new Student instance. It has no name attribute yet, and student has not been assigned.
Enter __init__. self points to the new instance, while the local parameter name holds "Ada".
Read the local parameter name on the right-hand side. It is separate from the instance attribute self.name.
Store "Ada" in the instance's name attribute. self still points to the same object.
__init__ finishes with None. The enclosing Student("Ada") constructor call produces the initialized instance, shown by its reference badge.
Bind student to the constructed instance. The initializer's local self and name no longer exist.
Read student.name from the instance. Dot notation accesses an attribute, rather than a dictionary key.
The console shows Ada. student still points to the Student instance with its name attribute.

conditional.caption: Look up age before comparing it with 18.
Evaluating 16 >= 18 gives False, a Boolean value.
The condition is false, so skip line 3 and enter the else branch.
Only the selected branch prints its message.

dictionary-fields.caption: Create a dictionary with two named fields. student points to this one object; name holds "Ada" and score holds 5.
The key "score" identifies the field to change. We will store 7 there while leaving "name" unchanged.
Replace the score field's value 5 with 7. The dictionary and student's reference keep the same identity.
Read the value stored under "score". The field supplies the integer 7 to print().
The console shows 7. The dictionary still has both fields, and name still holds "Ada".

function-call.caption: Store 10 in the global variable value. Defining the function did not run its body.
Look up the argument before calling add_one().
Enter add_one(). Its parameter value is local to this new call frame.
Inside the function, value refers to the local parameter. The global value is separate.
Adding 1 to the local value gives 11.
Store 11 in result, another variable local to this call.
Look up the local result to return it.
Return 11 to the caller. The function frame and its local variables are removed.
Store the returned number in the global variable answer. The global value is still 10.
Look up answer for the final output.
The console shows 11. The local result existed only while the function was running.

hello-world.caption: The arrow marks the line we are about to run. print() sends a message to the console.
The console shows Hello, world! The quotation marks belong to the code; they are not part of the printed message.

instance-method.caption: Begin with ada pointing to a Student named "Ada". This setup step summarizes construction and initialization.
Summarize construction of a second Student named "Grace". The two instances have independent state.
ada identifies the instance receiving the method call. Evaluate "Lovelace" for the new_name argument.
Enter rename. The receiver ada becomes the local self reference; new_name holds "Lovelace". Both ada and self point to student-1.
Read the local parameter new_name. The instance's name attribute still holds "Ada".
Update the instance through self. ada sees the same object's new name, while grace's separate instance stays unchanged.

rename reaches the end without an explicit return, so the call's result is None. Its locals disappear, but the attribute change remains. Unlike construction, this call does not produce an instance reference.
The unused None result is discarded. Read "Lovelace" through ada, which still points to student-1.
Print the name changed by the method.
Read grace's name from student-2. The method was called on ada, so this instance still holds "Grace".
The outputs show the method's lasting change to one instance. Its None result was not printed or assigned.

list-aliasing.caption: Create one list. The name numbers points to it; list-1 is our label for this object.
Bind other to the same list. Both arrows point to list-1; no second list is created.
We will append 6 through other. Predict what printing numbers will show.
Change the shared list to [2, 4, 6]. The two names still point to the same object.
Through numbers, we can see the new element at index 2. It is the very same list.
Read the list through numbers, even though the append used other.
The console shows [2, 4, 6]. Assignment gave the list another name; it did not copy its contents.

list-append.caption: Create a list with two elements, at indices 0 and 1.
The value to append is 6. It will go after the existing elements.
Add 6 at the end. The list grows from two elements to three.
The new element has index 2. The original cells keep their values and indices.
Read the whole list after appending.
The console shows [2, 4, 6]. Step backward to restore the two-element list.

list-copying.caption: Create a list and bind numbers to it. Its teaching label is list-1.
copy() creates a second list with the same contents. The two names now point to different objects.
We will append 6 through other. Predict what printing each list will show.
Only list-2 grows to [2, 4, 6]. The original list-1 remains [2, 4].
The new element at index 2 belongs to the copy. Equal starting contents did not make these the same object.
Read the original list through numbers. It still contains just 2 and 4.
Printing numbers shows [2, 4]; appending to the copy left it unchanged.
Read the separate list through other. This is the one we changed.
Printing other shows [2, 4, 6]. Compare this with assignment alone, where both names pointed to one list.

list-iteration.caption: The list contains three elements. Their positions are numbered 0, 1, and 2.
Start the running total at zero.
The loop reads the first element, at index 0. Its value is 2.
Bind n to the element's value, 2. n is not the index.
Add the current element to the total. 0 + 2 gives 2.
Store 2 in total. Reading the element did not change the list.
Advance to index 1. The next element's value is 4.
n becomes 4; total retains 2 from the previous iteration.
The running total becomes 6. The list still contains 2, 4, and 6.
Advance to the final element, at index 2. Its value is 6.
n becomes 6. The index is 2, while the element's value is 6.
There are no more elements. Leave the loop; Python keeps n at its last value, 6.
Read the final total to print it.
The console shows 12, the sum of the list's three elements.

list-removal.caption: Create a list with three elements at indices 0, 1, and 2.
Index 1 selects the second element, whose value is 4.
Delete that element. The list shrinks to two cells; 6 moves from index 2 to index 1.
Index 1 now refers to 6. Its value did not change; its position did.
Read the shorter list. There is no empty cell or gap at the removed position.
The console shows [2, 6]. Step backward to restore 4 and the original indices.

list-update.caption: Create a list with three elements at indices 0, 1, and 2.
Index 1 selects the second element, currently 4. The new value is 10.
Replace the element at index 1 with 10. Only this cell changes.
The list is now [2, 10, 6]. Its length is still three, and indices 0 and 2 retain their values.
Read the whole updated list to print it.
The console shows the updated list. Step backward to compare it with the original.

naming-value.caption: Assignment binds the name score to the integer 5. The Variables panel shows its current value.
Read score to find the value that print() will use. The name refers to 5; it is not the message to print.
The console shows 5. Reading score did not change its stored value.

nested-function-call.caption: Store 10 globally. Neither function body has run yet.
Look up the argument for double_after_bump().
The outer call gets its own local parameter value. The global value stays separate.
The outer function passes its local value to add_one(). Its result is not assigned yet.
The outer frame pauses at line 6 while add_one() runs in a new frame.
This value belongs to add_one(). Each call has a separate parameter with the same name.
Add 1 to the inner parameter to get 11.
Create result in the inner frame. The paused outer frame still has no result.
Read the inner result for the first return.
Return 11 to line 6. Only add_one() finishes; the outer frame resumes.
Store the returned 11 in the outer frame's own result variable.
Read the outer result. The inner frame has already gone.
Double the returned value to get 22.
Update the outer result to 22. The global value remains 10.
Read the outer result for the second return.
Return 22 to line 11. Both calls have now finished, and no function frames remain.
Assign the final returned value to the global answer.
Look up the global answer for printing.
The console shows 22. Step backward across each return to restore that call's locals.

numeric-input.caption: input() shows its prompt and waits for the user to type something.
The user types 30 and presses Enter.
input() always gives back a string, even when the user types digits.
The string "30" is stored in the variable text.
Python looks up text and finds the string "30".
int() converts the string "30" into the integer 30.
Now age holds a number, so we can do math with it.
Because age is an int, 100 - age works out to 70.
The f-string fills in 70 and print() shows the message.

runtime-error.caption: This program can begin executing. First it reaches a print statement.
The console records Starting before anything fails.
Store the string "abc" in age. Assigning a string is valid.
Read age before trying to convert it to an integer. years has not been assigned yet.
The conversion fails before assignment. age and the earlier output remain, but years is never created and the final print statement is not reached.

simple-arithmetic.caption: Before print() can show anything, Python evaluates the addition inside the parentheses. What is 2 + 3?
The expression 2 + 3 evaluates to the integer 5. The badge shows that result beside the code.
print() sends the result to the console. The output is 5, rather than the expression 2 + 3.

strings-and-numbers.caption: These operands are integers. Predict the result of adding 2 and 3.
Integer addition gives 5. The int tag identifies the result as a number.
Quotation marks make these operands strings. What will joining "2" and "3" produce?
For strings, + joins the text. The result is "23", with a str tag; it is not integer addition.
The second console line shows 23 without quotation marks. The badge showed its string type; console text alone does not show that distinction.

syntax-error.caption: The if statement is missing its colon. Python cannot begin executing this program, so even the earlier age assignment has not happened.

two-instances.caption: The Student definition is already available. Each new instance will have its own name attribute.
Evaluate "Ada" for the first constructor call.
Allocate the first Student. Its name attribute has not been initialized yet.
In this initializer call, self points to student-1 and the local name is "Ada".
Read this call's local name parameter.
Initialize student-1's name to "Ada" through self.
The initializer finishes with None; the constructor expression produces a reference to student-1.
Bind ada to the first instance. The initializer's locals are gone.
Evaluate "Grace" for a separate constructor call using the same class.
Allocate a second Student with a distinct identity. student-1 still holds "Ada".
This new call has its own locals. self now points to student-2, while ada still points to student-1.
Read "Grace" from the second initializer's local name parameter.
Initialize student-2's name to "Grace". The first instance's name remains "Ada".
The second initializer finishes with None; this constructor expression produces a reference to student-2.
ada and grace point to two independent instances of the same class. Both have an attribute named name.
Evaluate the replacement name before updating ada's instance.
Replace only student-1's name with "Lovelace". Using the same class and attribute name does not make the two instances share that attribute's value.
Follow ada's reference and read "Lovelace" from the first instance.
Print the first instance's updated name.
Follow grace's different reference. Its instance still holds "Grace".
The two outputs confirm independent state. Updating ada.name did not change grace.name.

while-loop.caption: Start count at 0. The loop will check count before running its body.
With count at 0, 0 < 2 is True. Enter the loop body.
Read count for the first print. Its value is 0.
Evaluate 0 + 1 to get 1. count still holds 0 until assignment.
Store 1 in count, then return to the condition at the top of the loop.
Now 1 < 2 is True. Run the body again with count at 1.
Read count for the second print. Its value is now 1.
Evaluate 1 + 1 to get 2. count still holds 1 until assignment.
Store 2 in count, then check the condition again.
Now 2 < 2 is False. Skip the body; there is no third iteration and no printed 2.
Leave the loop and continue at the unindented print after it. count remains 2.
The console shows 0, 1, then Done. The final false condition ended the loop.
